section_summaries.epidemiology: Sarcocystis parasites are a rare cause of eosinophilic enteritis, subcutaneous nodules, and eosinophilic myositis. Humans are definitive hosts for Sarcocystis hominis and S. suihominis, which cause intestinal sarcocystosis from consuming uncooked beef or pork, typically asymptomatically. Humans can also be dead-end intermediate hosts for non-human Sarcocystis spp. after accidental ingestion of oocysts, leading to muscular sarcocystosis. Most human cases are described from Southeast Asia, but Sarcocystis has a worldwide distribution and is likely underrecognized.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: Sarcocystis parasites are obligatory, two-host, intracellular coccidian parasites. S. hominis and S. suihominis use humans as definitive hosts, causing intestinal sarcocystosis. Humans can also become dead-end intermediate hosts for non-human Sarcocystis spp. after ingesting oocysts. The life cycle involves sporocysts rupturing in the intermediate host, releasing sporozoites that undergo schizogony in endothelial cells, then merozoites invade myocytes to form sarcocysts. There is no evidence of sarcocyst rupture initiating new replication in the intermediate host.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: Human disease can manifest as either an enteric or muscular infection. Enteric infections are often asymptomatic or cause mild, self-limited symptoms like nausea, abdominal discomfort, and diarrhea, with rapid onset (3-6 hours) and resolution within 36 hours. Muscular sarcocystosis, usually asymptomatic, can present with fever, myalgias, bronchospasm, fleeting pruritic rashes, transient lymphadenopathy, subcutaneous nodules, eosinophilia, and elevated hepatic enzymes and muscle creatinine kinase in symptomatic cases.
section_summaries.diagnosis: Intestinal sarcocystosis is diagnosed by visualizing sporulated sporocysts or oocysts in stool specimens using flotation procedures. Definitive diagnosis of Sarcocystis myositis is by muscle biopsy, requiring differentiation from other muscle cyst-forming organisms like Toxoplasma gondii and Trypanosoma cruzi. Sarcocysts are septate with a distinct cell wall. In the absence of a muscle biopsy, eosinophilia with a compatible clinical syndrome and epidemiologic exposure supports a probable diagnosis; serology is of uncertain value.
section_summaries.treatment: Treatment for Sarcocystis organisms in muscle and intestine is considered unsatisfactory as they are terminal stages and will not spread to new cells. No specific treatment for Sarcocystis infection has been described. Treatment is symptomatic and palliative; corticosteroids may alleviate episodic allergic inflammatory reactions or chronic systemic symptoms. Cotrimoxazole, if initiated early, may shorten symptoms in some muscular infections. There is no risk of recrudescence.
section_summaries.prevention: Muscle involvement can be prevented by avoiding food and water contaminated with feces of predatory carnivores, with boiling water being preventive. Enteric infection can be prevented by avoiding ingestion of raw or undercooked beef and pork. Sporocysts are hardy, resisting treatment with bleach, chlorhexidine, and iodophor Betadine, but most frozen (-20°C) or well-cooked meats are safe.
